# DG (Dollar General) — Value Investor Note

## Circle of Competence
Simple to understand: small-box discount retail selling consumables and household basics to a price-sensitive, disproportionately rural and lower-income customer. No exotic technology risk, no complex financial engineering. The real question isn't whether the business model is legible — it is — but whether its historically defensive, recession-resistant reputation still holds when operating margin has already been cut nearly in half from its peak.

## Moat & Durability — Score 5/10
DG's edge is real-estate density: thousands of small-format stores in towns too thin to support two dollar-store or grocery formats, defended further by a lean, low-cost distribution network built around that footprint. That is a genuine structural advantage over larger-box competitors who can't profitably serve the same geography. But it buys almost no pricing power — gross margin sits at 30.8%, operating margin at just 5.9%, both compressed from historical highs by shrink (theft/loss), wage inflation, and Walmart's aggressive grocery pricing plus Aldi's expansion directly into DG's rural/exurban turf. A moat that shows up in store count but not in margin trend is a moat under real pressure, not a settled one — hence 5, not higher.

## Management & Capital Allocation
ROE of 18.9% is respectable on its face, but it sits on top of debt/equity near 179%. The packet doesn't disaggregate financial debt from ASC 842 capitalized operating-lease liabilities, which are structurally large for any retailer leasing ~20,000 stores — so it's impossible to tell from here how much of that leverage is benign lease accounting versus real financial risk. What is visible: a multi-year run of CEO turnover before Todd Vasos's return, a genuine governance/continuity concern this data can't paper over. Free cash flow yield of 7.2% is funding the dividend and a curtailed buyback program while the company works through a cooler-door and remodel capex cycle — a reasonable, if constrained, capital-allocation posture for a business mid-turnaround rather than one compounding from strength. The market's own forward P/E discount to trailing (14.8x vs. 16.8x) signals some expected margin recovery, which is a forecast, not a fact in evidence.

## Predictability
Revenue growth of 3.4% and an operating margin roughly half its historical peak describe a business searching for a bottom, not a steady compounder — this fails Munger's 'easy decision' bar even though the business model itself is simple. Momentum data underscores the market's own uncertainty: -18.2% over six months, then a +14.6% three-month bounce, RSI a neutral 58.3, price still -2.9% below the 200-day average, and a composite momentum score of 47 (dead center of the range). The packet's thesis field is null, so there's no qualitative overlay beyond price action — and that price action reads as unresolved, not confirmed turnaround.

## Inversion — How an Owner Loses Money From Here
1. **Margin doesn't actually recover**: shrink, wage inflation, and Walmart/Aldi price competition keep operating margin pinned near 5-6% rather than returning to the historical 8-9% range, permanently lowering normalized owner earnings below what today's multiple assumes.
2. **Leverage turns a soft patch into a hard one**: at ~179% debt/equity, a shock to DG's lower-income core customer — SNAP benefit reductions, a broader consumer pullback — hits equity value disproportionately given the thin cushion above the debt/lease load.
3. **The turnaround stalls on execution**: further leadership instability or a remodel/DG Fresh capex program that fails to lift comparable-store sales would confirm the market's existing skepticism rather than surprise it — the multiple has room to compress further, not just re-rate up.

## Valuation
The packet provides market cap ($26.14B), trailing P/E (16.76x), forward P/E (14.77x), and FCF yield (7.2%) but not share count or share price. Backing into per-share terms using an approximate ~205M diluted share count (a modeling assumption, not sourced from the packet) implies a current price near $127.50, trailing EPS near $7.61, forward EPS near $8.63, and FCF/share near $9.18.

Blending trailing and forward EPS into a normalized owner-earnings range of roughly $8.00-$8.60/share, and applying a Munger-conservative 13x-17x multiple (below the market's own 14.8x-16.8x range, to reflect the leverage and margin uncertainty flagged above rather than assume the turnaround succeeds):
- **Low case**: 13x × $8.00 ≈ $104/share
- **High case**: 17x × $8.60 ≈ $146/share

Midpoint ~$125/share versus an implied current price of ~$127.50/share is roughly a wash — margin of safety of about -2%. That is not a margin of safety in the Graham/Buffett sense; the stock is priced for the turnaround to work, not for a cushion if it doesn't.

## The Cloning Caveat
Richard Pzena (Pzena Investment Management, a classic deep-value shop) added 48.2% to an existing position, landing at 1.12% of portfolio — a real, building conviction signal from a manager whose whole discipline is buying statistically cheap, out-of-favor names, though 1.12% is a moderate, not maximal, sizing. First Pacific Advisors opened a brand-new position sized at just 0.02% of portfolio — functionally a rounding-error starter stake, not a statement. Ruane Cunniff LP (Sequoia Fund's manager, part of the Buffett-adjacent value lineage) added but the position rounds to 0.0% of portfolio — immaterial. Read together: this is mild, not strong, corroboration — one value investor building a real if modest stake, two others barely dipping a toe. It supports doing the work on DG, but it is not a cluster of high-conviction bets that should move the needle on its own.

## Verdict
**Watch, conviction 3/10.** DG is an understandable, structurally-advantaged-but-thinning-moat business genuinely mid-turnaround: margins have been cut nearly in half from peak, leverage is elevated (with the lease-vs-debt mix opaque from this packet), and management continuity was shaky until recently. At an implied ~$127.50/share, the price is roughly in line with a conservative owner-earnings estimate — there is no real margin of safety here, and Munger-strict discipline says most things, including this one at today's price, are a pass on valuation grounds. The business is worth tracking for a better entry (a larger pullback, or confirmed margin recovery that would justify paying up), but it does not clear the bar to buy today.
momentum_thesis: DG's twelve-month tape nets to a flat +4.7%, but the path underneath is the real story: a brutal six-month air pocket (-18.2%) followed by a sharp three-month reclaim (+14.7%), now cooling with a -3.3% pullback over the past month. RSI14 at 58 and price sitting essentially on the 200DMA (-2.9%) put this squarely in "testing the trendline" territory — no overbought excess, no confirmed breakout, just a name deciding whether the 200-day flips from resistance to support. Positioning offers little squeeze fuel: short interest is thin at 3.9% of float with only 3.1 days to cover, so the bounce is being driven by fundamental buyers rather than shorts capitulating, and the call-tilted put/call OI (0.75) confirms modestly constructive but unstretched options sentiment. The superinvestor tape backs the reversal read — Pzena, a deep-value shop, added 48% to an already-material 1.1%-of-portfolio stake in Q2, the kind of sizing-up that signals conviction bought into the drawdown, while FPA's new 0.02%-of-portfolio starter and Ruane Cunniff's ~0%-weight add are too small to carry independent signal. Beta of 0.235 keeps this an idiosyncratic, company-specific story rather than a macro-momentum play — a defensive discount-retailer turnaround thesis, not a high-beta momentum trade. Net: constructive but unconfirmed — a stock that has stopped falling and is attracting value capital, but hasn't yet proven the bounce is more than a bounce.
